newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's sale of historical site stirs dismay.
newsitem.headline: France's sale of historical site stirs dismay.

text.p: Local authorities in Verdun, site of one of the bloodiest battles of World War One, expressed dismay on Monday after France's Defence Ministry publicly advertised to sell the town's historical Citadel fort.

"Putting the Citadel on sale on the Minitel is indecent. If anyone can go about transforming it into who knows what, what will remain of its past?" said Dominique Peridont, who heads the tourist office in the eastern French town.
The Minitel is France's highly popular public computer network, which predates the Internet by years.

Nearly half a million people visit the Verdun battlefields each year, a major source of income for the town. Some 150,000 of them also visit the Citadel and its several kilometres (miles) of underground tunnels, where the tourism office runs a profitable war museum.
The 18th-century fort is being sold as part of a military reform ending conscription and making the French army into a smaller, all-professional unit.
The Citadel has been for sale for nearly three years but it is only in the past few days that the sale began to be widely advertised to the public on the Minitel network.
Military authorities said they would exercise control over the sale and expected the new owners to keep open the museum.
The tourism office currently pays part of its annual revenues from the museum to the Defence Ministry as rent.
During the protracted 1916 battle in which 175,000 French and 165,000 German soldiers were killed, the Citadel was a French headquarters.

It is best known because the body of France's unknown soldier was selected there in 1920 from among eight unidentified bodies brought from major World War One battlefields before being placed under theArc de Triomphe in Paris.
